strengths: Pareto-set identification on continuous design spaces under noisy evaluations has an identifiable audience in Bayesian optimization and active learning. Adaptive discretization combined with a multi-output GP offers useful ideas for this audience.

Regional confidence bounds and their inheritance across refinements provide a coherent algorithmic approach. Analyzing both information-gain and metric-dimension complexity, while accommodating dependent objectives, is a worthwhile contribution.

Pseudocode, illustrations, and detailed appendices help explain the proposed approach. The experiments consider complementary performance metrics, and Table 2 transparently reports the computational cost of the theoretical depth setting.
weaknesses: Necessary: Resolve gaps in the central confidence and sample-complexity arguments. Corollary 1 defines V_h using log(h²) while including h=0. Substituting its chosen u into Lemma 7 also produces 2h log N, whereas the stated V_h contains h log N. In Lemma 14, equations (32) and (34) apply the parent's refinement condition at the current evaluation count; this does not follow from an earlier refinement because β grows. These issues leave the stated guarantees insufficiently justified, even if corrected arguments may be possible.

Necessary: Specify consistent handling of ties in Definition 10. Weak dominance excludes both nodes when their lower confidence corners coincide, so the pessimistic Pareto set can be empty even when other nodes have strictly inferior lower corners. Lemma 3 assumes that a dominating pessimistic member exists. Inherited confidence rectangles make ties relevant to the algorithm. The termination and coverage arguments need to address this case explicitly.

Necessary: Example 1 does not establish the claimed separation between the bounds. On page 20, the lower bound has the form γ_T ≥ T c_T, where c_T depends on the decreasing coefficients and can approach zero; this does not imply Ω(T). Keeping the amplitudes bounded away from zero creates infinitely many points separated in the GP-induced metric, conflicting with compactness and the Hölder condition in Assumption 1. An admissible separating example is needed, or the linear-information-gain and incomparability claims should be withdrawn.

Necessary: Align empirical coverage with the formal guarantee. Section 6.1.3 measures proximity within 2ε of a predicted point, whereas Definition 4 requires componentwise ε-domination. Consequently, 100% reported coverage does not establish an ε-cover. The nearest-point accuracy description also needs reconciliation with Definition 3. Specify the distance used, how regional outputs and baseline outputs become evaluated point sets, and the observation-noise variance.

Necessary: Correct specific unsupported empirical claims and presentation errors. Section 1.1 claims experimental improvements over ε-PAL, but Section 6 compares against PESMO, ParEGO, and USeMO without reporting ε-PAL results. Supply that comparison or remove the claim. Additionally, the two Matérn panels in Figure 11 duplicate the plotted curves and error bars despite apparently representing different input dimensions; this requires correction or explanation. Define the error bars and distinguish single-run illustrations from repeated-run evidence.

Optional: Experiments with correlated objectives and kernel misspecification would broaden practical understanding. Repeating the depth-cap comparison would also help: the approximately 900-fold acceleration in Table 2 uses the explicitly non-theoretical modification V_h=0 beyond a shallow cap, whose reliability is illustrated on only one setup.
